tl;dr version: with diesel, you enemy is moisture. Keep out water and keep out humid air. With gasoline, your enemy is evaporation. Seal it and seal it tight with the least amount of air in the can.

On taxes -- It's diesel specific. Diesel and Home Fuel Oil are the same chemical. Oil boilers burn the same diesel as trucks. But, they also include road taxes in the cost of diesel at the filling station. There's no reason to pay road taxes to heat your home, so that isn't included if you run fuel oil. They are two separate distribution chains.

The thing is, people are smart enough to know that they can take the oil from the fuel oil drum and put it in their trucks -- especially huge trucking companies. So, to show that the fuel came from a filling station (and paid the taxes) they dye the diesel red, so a state trooper can look in the tank and see the red fuel. If it's clear, that trucker is in trouble. On the other hand, if you are on farm plates running a truck on the farm, you are allowed to burn fuel oil instead of taxed diesel.

Not all of the dyes are the red tax dye. There is also a green dye that the military uses. You can get in biiiiig big trouble if you are driving off a US military base and they sample your diesel and it's green (or purple).

Part 2 -- gas:

Diesel and gas are very different and store differently. Diesel is relatively easy to store. It doesn't have many volatiles to evaporate out, so your main danger is water. Protecting the cans from corrosion would be your biggest threat. If it corrodes below the fuel line, you lose that much fuel wherever it corrodes through and then you are allowing moisture in. Moisture won't hurt the diesel so much (it will actually settle out) but it will allow bacteria to live that literally eat the hydrocarbons and ruin the diesel. So water is bad and oxygen isn't good, because they allow the bacteria to thrive.

With gasoline, your main problem is the violates that evaporate out. BTEX (Benzene, toluene, ethylbenzene and xylene IIRC) are what gives you the high octane of gasoline. The difference between regular and supreme is how much BTEX it has in it. BTEX is what you are smelling when you sniff gas (specifically the toluene, the stuff in airplane glue). To store gas, you have to keep that stuff in the gas and out of the air. That's where sealed cans and being full comes in. If there is very little air and that air isn't changing, it can saturate with a little BTEX and then the rest stays in the fuel. That's why the good seal (and that giant clamp on jerry cans) is so important -- there is positive vapor pressure in the gas trying to drive that seal open.
